title: Vayikra: the small alef (Leviticus 1:1)
hook: the first word is written with a small letter; midrash sees Moses' humility

segments.voice: Yesterday, the book where children once began: let the pure study the pure. Your line was begin with the pure. What did you start fresh? Day three hundred eighty.

A Torah scroll is written by hand, on parchment, by a trained scribe, letter by letter. The rules are strict. Every letter must be complete, every space the right size, and a scribe copies from a checked text rather than from memory. One wrong letter can make a scroll unfit to read in public. So when one letter in the scroll is written noticeably smaller than the letters around it, that's not a slip of the pen. It's on purpose, a scribal tradition handed down from scribe to scribe. And it's in the very first word of Leviticus.
screen: `WRITTEN BY HAND, LETTER BY LETTER.` → `ONE WRONG LETTER MATTERS.` → `ONE LETTER, WRITTEN SMALL.`

segments.voice: The word is vayikra, and He called, and the small letter is its last one, an alef. The scribal tradition keeps it small, and the Torah itself never explains why. So the commentators asked. One answer comes from the medieval commentator known as the Baal HaTurim. Take the alef off, he points out, and vayikra becomes vayikar: and He happened upon, as if by chance. That's the word the Torah uses when God appears to Balaam, the prophet for hire. Moses, the story goes, was so humble that he wanted to write his own call the same way, as if God had only bumped into him. God told him to write the alef. So Moses wrote it, but small. Another teaching sets it beside a large alef in the Bible: the first letter of Adam's name, at the start of the book of Chronicles, is written big. In that teaching, Adam, made by God's own hands, grew too sure of himself, while Moses, who spoke with God face to face, made himself small. The Torah does call Moses humble. In the JPS 1917 translation: "Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men that were upon the face of the earth." It's worth noticing what the humility isn't. Moses doesn't refuse the call or leave out the letter. He goes into the tent, he does the work, he writes the word. He just doesn't make the letter any bigger than it needs to be. In this reading, humility means taking up the space the task needs, and no more: a letter at the size the word requires.
screen: `THE ALEF OF VAYIKRA, WRITTEN SMALL.` · `VAYIKAR: AS IF BY CHANCE.` · `ADAM'S BIG ALEF, MOSES' SMALL ONE.` · `MOSES WAS VERY MEEK.` · then, large: `THE SMALL LETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make yourself a little smaller. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place in your life where you tend to take up a lot of room: a meeting where you talk first, a family conversation you steer, a group chat where you always have the last word. Picture yourself there today, still present, still doing your part, but a little smaller. Asking one question instead of making one point. Letting someone else go first. Breathe with that picture. The bell holds the time.
Vayikra. And He called. The first word of Leviticus, whose final alef scribes write small.
Your line: the small letter. Today, in one conversation, take up a little less room, and see who fills it. Day three hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Torah scribes write the final alef of vayikra smaller than the surrounding letters, following the scribal tradition, and printed Hebrew Bibles often reproduce it.

fork.setup: you're Moses, writing the word for how God called you into the tent. you'd rather not make a big deal of it. what do you do?
options: leave out the alef, so it reads 'happened upon'.
fork.reveal: in the Baal HaTurim's telling, God wouldn't let Moses leave it out, so he wrote it small. humble, but still answering the call.

original.note: Hebrew: alef, the first letter of the alphabet, written small at the end of vayikra.

trapdoor: what you thought: a typo in an old scroll.
what it means: a letter written small on purpose, read as a picture of Moses' humility.
what a scholar hears: the Baal HaTurim on Leviticus 1:1 contrasts vayikra with vayikar (Numbers 23:4, Balaam); a midrashic tradition pairs it with the large alef of Adam in 1 Chronicles 1:1.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed 'in every kosher scroll' and 'for centuries' (unsourced); 'best-known answer' softened; the Adam/Moses contrast framed as that teaching's reading; replaced a stock humility aphorism with a line drawn from the letter itself.
Numbers 12:3 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording.
Baal HaTurim on Leviticus 1:1 (Moses wanted to write vayikar; God insisted; he wrote the alef small): confirm.
The pairing with the large alef of Adam (1 Chronicles 1:1) is a later homiletic tradition; confirm the source and that the large alef is standard in the Masorah.
Closing reading ('humility is taking up the space your task needs') is the script's own framing, not attributed to a source.
